unrequested_advice.span: Give it a reasonable pause (a few days to a week), then follow up.
Don’t catch them in passing again.
Send a calendar invite or ask to book 15 minutes specifically about “compensation” or “performance review.”
When you do circle back, bring your evidence: accomplishments, market data, value delivered, and a clear request.

valence.span: The phrase itself isn’t a no — but the way he delivered it suggests you’ll need to actively drive the follow-up.
valence.label: neutral

readings.span: It’s a common corporate phrase that means “we’ll discuss this later” or “let’s revisit this topic at another time.”
It usually means they’re not ready or willing to have the conversation right now.
They may have been caught off guard or don’t want to give an immediate answer.
They might need to check budgets, get approval, or consult with higher-ups before saying anything.
This is often how managers buy time when they don’t have authority to approve on the spot.

valence.span: In short, the poem is a quiet, radical manifesto: **Stop overthinking. Look at the world. Find the extraordinary in the ordinary. That attention is what everything depends on.**
valence.label: optimistic

readings.span: The poem is arguing that beauty and significance can be found in the ordinary world if we simply look closely enough.
The meaning is the aesthetic pleasure and clarity of that single, frozen moment.
It represents the unseen, physical labor that sustains life.
The poem finds a moment of perfect, harmonious coexistence between the manufactured and the natural world.
Ultimately, what "so much depends / upon" might be the act of perception itself.
